name: Vantage
tagline: The CISO's operating system: see far, decide well, lead calmly
description: A personal operating system for a CISO or security executive: daily rituals, the review rhythm, top risks, decisions, exceptions, stakeholders, team, KPIs and KRIs, playbooks and visible progress. Offline first.
audience: A CISO, a deputy, or any executive who owns security risk
north_star: Risks really reduced, decisions made on time, a team that grows, and a leader who keeps their energy. Not paperwork.
welcome: Vantage guides your week as a security leader: what needs you today, the reviews that keep the programme honest, and the progress you can show. Everything stays on this device unless you pair it with your estate.

principles.name: Pareto
principles.text: A few risks carry most of the exposure. Fix those first, and the basics before anything advanced.

principles.name: Inversion
principles.text: Ask what could end the organisation, and remove that downside before chasing upside.

principles.name: Control the inputs
principles.text: You cannot control attackers. You control decisions, rhythm and follow-through.

principles.name: Compounding
principles.text: A weekly review kept for a year beats a perfect plan kept for a month.

principles.name: Flywheel
principles.text: Visibility earns trust, trust earns budget, budget builds capability, capability earns more trust.

principles.name: Ikigai
principles.text: Lead where your strengths meet what the organisation needs; it keeps you going for years, not quarters.

principles.name: Antifragility
principles.text: Every incident and near miss leaves a lesson, a change and a drill. The programme gets stronger from stress.

principles.name: Small wins, shown
principles.text: Progress people can see keeps them, and you, going.

goals.intro: At most three goals a quarter. Each moves a number from where you are to where you need to be, by a date.
goals.placeholder: e.g. Prove we can recover from ransomware

krs.t: Critical and high findings past SLA

starter.o: Prove we can recover from ransomware

krs.t: Critical systems restored from the offline copy in a drill
Critical data covered by offline, tested backups

starter.o: Get full value from the tools we already pay for

krs.t: Licensed key features switched on and watched

starter.o: Make security visible and trusted at the top

krs.t: Board or committee reports with the 40,000-ft table
Business heads met one-to-one this quarter

starter.o: Build a team that does not depend on one person

krs.t: Team members with a growth plan

rituals.intro: Six small habits that carry the job. Each has a trigger and a two-minute floor: on a bad day, the floor counts.

items.name: Threat and alert brief
items.anchor: IF I open the laptop THEN I read the overnight SOC summary before email
items.min: Read the one-line summary of the top three alerts.
items.why: You hear about trouble from your team first, not from the news.

items.name: One risk decision
items.anchor: IF a risk or exception waits on me THEN I decide, delegate or date it today
items.min: Write down who owns it and by when.
items.why: Undecided risk is accepted risk that nobody signed for.

items.name: One stakeholder touch
items.anchor: IF I have a gap between meetings THEN I ask one business leader what worries them
items.min: Send one message: what worries you this month?
items.why: Security that business leaders call early is security that works.

items.name: Unblock one person
items.anchor: IF I see my team in the morning THEN I ask one person what is blocking them
items.why: Your team's speed is your speed.

items.name: Think and learn
items.anchor: IF it is after lunch THEN 20 minutes of reading or thinking, phone face down
items.min: Read one page or one advisory.
items.why: Strategy needs quiet time; the urgent never leaves any.

items.name: Shut down
items.anchor: IF I close the laptop THEN I write tomorrow's top three
items.min: One line: the one thing that must happen tomorrow.
items.why: A clear stop protects your evening and your judgement.

wheel.intro: Score each area honestly once a quarter: 10 is leading practice, 5 is 'it works on a good day', 1 is missing. Put the next goal in the lowest area.

dims.label: Governance and strategy
dims.hint: Policy current, strategy approved, roles clear, the Board engaged.
dims.lever: Write the strategy on one page and get it approved.

dims.label: Risk and compliance
dims.hint: Top risks known, owned and dated; obligations mapped; audit points closing.
dims.lever: Give every high risk an owner and a treatment date this week.

dims.label: People and skills
dims.hint: Enough people, the right skills, a deputy for every key role, including you.
dims.lever: Size the team with ./securax govern team and fill the basics first.

dims.label: Process and operations
dims.hint: Vulnerability SLAs, change, exceptions and access reviews run without you.
dims.lever: Start with the vulnerability SLA and the exception register.

dims.label: Technology and architecture
dims.hint: The basics deployed and used: EDR, MFA, patching, logging. Tools tuned, not shelfware.
dims.lever: Run the tool value check: switch on what you already pay for.

dims.label: Detection and response
dims.hint: Alerts watched round the clock, playbooks tested, time to respond falling.
dims.lever: Run one tabletop this quarter and fix what it finds.

dims.label: Resilience and recovery
dims.hint: Offline backups restored in a drill; BCP and DR tested; the crisis team rehearsed.
dims.lever: Restore one critical system from the offline copy, and time it.

dims.label: Stakeholders and Board
dims.hint: Business leaders call security early; the Board gets a clear, honest picture.
dims.lever: Meet two business heads this month and ask what worries them.

dims.label: You: energy and growth
dims.hint: Sleep, focus, learning, time away. A tired CISO makes slow decisions.
dims.lever: Protect one morning a week for thinking.

cadence.intro: The reviews that keep a programme honest. Anything due or late rises to Today by itself.

items.name: Monday risk and priority review
items.why: Thirty minutes that stop surprises.
checklist: Top risks: did any move? Is any high risk without an owner or a date?
Critical and high findings past SLA: who closes which this week?
Exceptions expiring in the next 30 days
Last week's incidents and near misses: one lesson each
Set the week's three priorities

items.name: Friday wins and lessons
items.why: Wins collected weekly make the monthly update write itself.
checklist: Write the week's three wins
One lesson, and what we change
Thank one person by name
Empty the inbox: decide every item

items.name: One-to-ones with direct reports
items.why: People stay for a leader who knows what blocks them.
checklist: Their goals and blockers
One skill to grow: a course, a certification or a range exercise
Recognise something specific

items.name: Management security update
items.why: One page a month keeps management with you.
checklist: KPIs and KRIs updated
Top five risks, each with owner and date
What was done and what it bought: risk reduced, money saved
The one ask of management
Send it as one page

items.name: Tool value check
items.why: Paid features left switched off are money spent on no protection.
checklist: For each major tool: is every licensed feature that matters switched on?
Are its alerts watched by someone, and tuned?
What share of assets does it really cover?
Did the vendor meet its SLA and support terms?
Anything paid for and unused goes on the renewal list

items.name: Vulnerability and patch SLA review
items.why: Old criticals on internet-facing systems are how most breaches start.
checklist: SLA compliance by severity
The oldest open criticals, with owners
Internet-facing assets first
Repeat findings: fix the root cause, not the instance

items.name: Privileged access sample review
items.why: Admin rights outlive the people who needed them.
checklist: Sample admin accounts: is each still needed?
Leavers removed within a working day?
Shared or generic accounts: owner named, password vaulted

items.name: Board or committee report
items.why: The Board funds what it understands.
checklist: Fill the 40,000-ft table (Govern template 12)
Maturity and the plan from ./securax govern
Anything outside the risk appetite?
Decisions and support needed from the Board
Record the decisions in the decision log

items.name: Quarter reset: goals and wheel
items.why: Honest grading beats optimistic plans.
checklist: Grade last quarter's goals honestly
Re-score the programme wheel
Set at most three goals, starting with the lowest area

items.name: Drill or tabletop exercise
items.why: A plan never rehearsed fails when it is needed.
checklist: Pick a scenario: ransomware, DDoS, insider, vendor breach
Run it with the crisis team (60 to 90 minutes)
Check the reporting clocks with ./securax incident
Log each lesson with an owner and a date

items.name: Third-party risk refresh
items.why: Many breaches arrive through a supplier.
checklist: Re-tier the critical vendors
Chase overdue assessments
Contracts: right to audit, breach notice, data location

items.name: Budget against plan
items.why: Show savings before you ask for more.
checklist: Spend against plan
Savings from tools retired or right-sized
Next asks with their 5W1H and cost band (./securax govern)

items.name: Restore test of critical backups
items.why: A backup is only real once it has been restored.
checklist: Restore one critical system from the offline copy
Time it against the recovery time objective
Keep the result as audit evidence

items.name: Policy review and approval
items.why: Policies drift from practice and from regulation.
checklist: Review the information security and cyber policies (Govern templates 01-08)
Check them against current regulations and standards
Approval by the Board or its committee recorded
Users re-acknowledge the acceptable use policy

items.name: Strategy and budget refresh
items.why: Land the plan before the budget cycle closes.
checklist: Re-run ./securax govern and refresh the one-page strategy (template 10)
Prepare the asks before the budget cycle opens
Agree the scorecard targets for the year

items.name: Full BCP and DR test
items.why: Proves the organisation, not only IT, can keep going.
checklist: Business-led scenario with real switchover where safe
Measure recovery times against targets
Fix the gaps; update the plan

items.name: Certification and regulatory self-assessment
items.why: Evidence gathered all year makes audit week calm.
checklist: Obligations mapped to controls
Evidence current for each control
Last audit's points closed or dated

items.name: Cyber insurance review
items.why: Know what is covered before you need it.
checklist: Cover against the top risks
Exclusions and the insurer's panel for incident response
Controls the insurer requires are really in place

items.name: Awareness and skills plan
items.why: People are the first line; skills are the second.
checklist: Awareness topics and phishing simulations for the year
Each team member's certification or course
Range exercises for the response team (./securax exercise)

registers.label: Top risks
registers.title: risk
registers.intro: The few risks that could really hurt, scored likelihood times impact (1-25). High risks without a date rise to Today.

fields.label: The risk, in business words
fields.placeholder: e.g. Ransomware stops core systems for three days

fields.label: Likelihood
fields.hint: 1 rare, 3 possible, 5 almost certain this year

fields.label: Impact
fields.hint: 1 minor, 3 serious, 5 could end the organisation

guide: Write each risk as cause, event and business effect.
The owner is the business head who loses if it happens.
Accepted risks keep a review date and a named approver.
Keep the list short: the top ten to twenty, not everything.

registers.label: Decision log
registers.title: decision
registers.intro: Write down every decision that matters: what, why, who decided and when to look again. It protects you and it teaches the team.

registers.label: Exceptions
registers.title: what
registers.intro: Every exception owned, justified, compensated and dated. Each rises to Today 30 days before it expires.

registers.label: Tools and value
registers.title: tool
registers.intro: What each security tool costs, what it covers and whether its key features are really on. It rises to Today 60 days before renewal.
registers.next_verb: Fix, keep or retire before renewal

registers.label: Stakeholders
registers.title: who
registers.intro: The people whose trust the programme needs. Each one rises to Today when the touch is due.

registers.label: Team
registers.title: who
registers.intro: Your direct reports and key people: their growth goal and when you last had a real one-to-one.

registers.label: Lessons
registers.title: what
registers.intro: Antifragility in practice: every incident, near miss or audit point leaves a lesson, a change and a drill.

scorecard.intro: Log a number when you have it; progress counts from your first value. KRIs warn early; KPIs show the programme working.

metrics.name: Critical and high findings past SLA
metrics.why: The single best early warning of a breach.

metrics.name: Critical vendors not assessed this year
Critical systems sending logs to the SIEM
Mean time to respond to a confirmed incident
Critical systems restored in a drill (12 months)
Licensed key features switched on and watched

playbooks.intro: Proven sequences for the moments that matter. Tick as you go; a half-done one reminds you after two weeks.

items.title: The first 90 days (or a fresh start)
items.when: New in the role, or resetting a programme.
steps: Weeks 1-2: meet every business head; ask what worries them and what security has cost them
Read the last audit reports, regulator observations and incident reports
Inventory assets, data, applications, vendors and tools (Govern template asset-inventory.csv)
Name the crown jewels: the few systems and data whose loss would hurt most
Score where you stand with ./securax govern: minimum basic against highest possible
List quick wins: high risk, low effort (MFA on admins, offline backups, internet-facing patching)
Check every paid tool: switched on, watched, covering what it should
Map the team: skills, gaps, single points of failure
Agree the risk appetite with senior management
Write the one-page strategy and 12-month roadmap (Govern template 10)
Present the 40,000-ft table to the Board (Govern template 12)
Set the rhythm: weekly risk review, monthly update, quarterly Board report

items.title: Reporting to the Board
items.when: Before every Board or committee meeting.
steps: One page, no jargon, trends rather than snapshots
Start with the three risks that matter, in business terms
What changed since last time: risks closed, maturity, incidents handled
The value: risk reduced, money saved, audit points closed
Be honest about what is not done yet, with dates
End with the decisions and the support you need
Record the Board's decisions in the decision log

items.title: Leading a major incident: the first hours
items.when: A serious incident is suspected or confirmed.
steps: Declare it, open the crisis team and name an incident lead (often not you)
Start the regulator reporting clocks: ./securax incident lists each deadline
Contain first, investigate second: isolate, and preserve evidence
Log every decision with the time and who decided
One voice outside: agree holding statements with communications and legal
Brief management on a fixed rhythm, for example every two to four hours
Decide early on outside help: forensics, the insurer's panel
Afterwards: an after-action review within two weeks; every lesson gets an owner and a drill

items.title: Building the budget and the business case
items.when: Before the budget cycle, or for any large ask.
steps: Start from the gaps: ./securax govern ranks them with their 5W1H and a cost band
Basics before advanced: never fund a showpiece while a basic is missing
For each ask: the risk it reduces, in money and in plain words
Count people and running costs, not only licences
Show savings first: tools retired, licences right-sized, overlaps removed
Get three quotes; check data location and support terms
Phase it: 0-3, 3-12 and 12-36 months
Agree the success measures (the scorecard) up front

items.title: Getting value from the tools you already pay for
steps: List every security tool with owner, cost and renewal date (Tools register)
For each: which key features are switched off, and why?
Is anyone watching its alerts? Is it tuned against false positives?
What share of assets does it actually cover?
Did the vendor meet its SLA and deliver the training it promised?
Fix, keep or retire before renewal, and record the saving
Raise vendor performance at the quarterly review

items.title: Making VAPT and application findings close
items.when: When findings pile up or keep coming back.
steps: One register for all findings, with closure SLAs by severity (Govern template 06)
Retest before closing; never close on a vendor's word alone
API security: use the checklist (Govern template 13) at design and before go-live
Fix the root cause of repeat findings with secure build standards
Report ageing and SLA compliance every month
Agree scope and rules of engagement before every test

items.title: Exceptions without regret
items.when: Whenever someone asks to skip a control.
steps: Every exception has an owner, a reason, a compensating control and an expiry
The risk owner approves it, not security alone
Review 30 days before expiry: renew with a reason, or close
Report the count and the expired ones every month

items.title: Audit and regulator readiness
items.when: All year, and a month before any audit.
steps: Map obligations to controls with ./securax comply
Collect evidence as you go, not the week before
Give each point from the last audit an owner and a date
Rehearse the walkthrough of your ten most important controls

items.title: Building the team
items.when: When the work outgrows the people.
steps: Size it with ./securax govern team
Hire for the basics first: governance and risk, vulnerability management, SOC oversight
Consultants lead in year one and train; your own team leads in year two
Every person has a growth goal and a skill to build (Team register)
Practise on the cyber range: ./securax exercise
Name a deputy: no single point of failure, including you

items.title: Looking after yourself
items.when: Always; read it when the job feels heavy.
steps: Protect one morning a week for thinking
Delegate decisions that do not need you; keep the decision log
Know your crisis handover: who leads when you are away
Take leave fully: the rhythm keeps running without you
Keep learning: one course or certification a year
